subject: Computer Networking
title: Firewalls: The First Wall
description: A quick win: understand Firewalls: The First Wall.

hook.text: A firewall sits between your network and the internet. It decides what gets in and what stays out.

buildup.text: Rules define allowed traffic by IP, port, and protocol. Anything not explicitly allowed is blocked by default.

discovery.text: Stateful firewalls track connections. They allow responses to your requests but block unsolicited inbound traffic.

twist.text: Firewalls can't inspect encrypted traffic without breaking the encryption. TLS makes deep inspection controversial.

climax.text: Next-gen firewalls add application awareness — they can block specific apps, not just ports.

punchline.text: A firewall is the bouncer. It checks the list before letting anyone in.

quiz.question: What does a stateful firewall track?
options: Active connections to allow legitimate responses
The physical location of all network devices

details.summary: Firewalls filter network traffic based on rules that define which connections are allowed or blocked. They sit at network boundaries, examining packets against configured policies for source, destination, port, and protocol. Modern firewalls add application awareness and deep packet inspection.
details.whyItMatters: Firewalls are the first layer of defense between trusted internal networks and the untrusted internet. A properly configured firewall blocks the vast majority of unauthorized access attempts.
takeaways: Firewalls enforce rules about what traffic can enter and leave
Stateful inspection tracks connection state for smarter filtering
Default-deny policies block everything not explicitly permitted

faq.question: What is a stateful firewall?
faq.answer: A stateful firewall tracks the state of active connections. It allows return traffic for established outbound connections without explicit rules. This is more secure and flexible than stateless packet filtering, which evaluates each packet independently without connection context.

faq.question: Should every network have a firewall?
faq.answer: Yes. Every network connected to the internet needs a firewall at the perimeter. Internal firewalls between network segments add defense in depth. Even cloud environments use virtual firewalls like security groups and network ACLs to control traffic flow between resources.
